title: Evaluating the MIRI TGT Governance Agenda's Technical Assumptions

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: testing empirical assumptions underlying a major governance strategy (compute restrictions) has direct implications for policymakers and organizations adopting that strategy.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: requires deep engagement with compute governance literature and the ability to evaluate empirical claims about semiconductor supply chains and compute tracking. Beyond typical beginner scope.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: identifying key assumptions, searching for existing evidence for each, and scoring each as supported/contested/unsupported. Tractable but requires substantial reading.

novelty.reasoning: MIRI TGT published its governance research agenda in May 2025, centered on international compute restrictions and an 'Off Switch' for frontier AI. The agenda makes explicit technical assumptions: training compute correlates with capabilities, FLOP thresholds can be set conservatively (10^24 FLOP cap), and compute can be monitored internationally. TGT's own paper 'Declare and Justify' argues evaluations should explicitly state assumptions. However, no external work has systematically evaluated the empirical validity of TGT's core assumptions (compute-capability correlation under algorithmic progress restrictions, semiconductor supply chain monitorability, enforcement feasibility). Apart Research ran a Technical AI Governance Challenge hackathon in early 2026 but no published output systematically tests these specific assumptions.

evidence: AI Governance to Avoid Extinction: The Strategic Landscape and Actionable Research Questions. MIRI TGT, May 2025.
Considerations for setting the FLOP thresholds in our example international AI agreement. MIRI TGT, 2025.
Declare and Justify: Explicit assumptions in AI evaluations are necessary for effective regulation. MIRI TGT.
